method.title: From orbit to one sentence

sections.title: Where the data comes from
body: Fire detections come from NASA FIRMS, from two instruments. MODIS, on the Terra and Aqua satellites, spots unusually hot points on the ground in pixels about 1 km wide. VIIRS, on the Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 (also called J1) satellites, does the same with pixels of 375 m, so it sees smaller fires and splits big ones into more points.

Pick MODIS or VIIRS at the top of the page. Each sensor is only compared with itself: a VIIRS month against other VIIRS months. The two counts are not added together, and VIIRS counts are much higher for the same fires.

We use the 2020–2024 FIRMS archive for Morocco, Australia and Brazil, for both sensors. Weather comes from NASA POWER, land cover from the MODIS MCD12Q1 product served by NASA GIBS, and open wildfires from NASA EONET.

sections.title: What we removed
body: We keep presumed vegetation fires only: volcanoes, fixed heat sources (factories, gas flares) and offshore detections are dropped.
We drop low-confidence detections: MODIS confidence below 30%, and VIIRS points flagged low.
We drop places that 'burn' more than 60 days a year for several years: those are industrial sites, not fires.

sections.title: How a month gets its level
body: Each month is compared with the same month in the other years, in the same country: July 2022 against the other Julys. The fire season is built in.
The year being tested is left out of its own comparison, so an extreme month cannot hide itself.
The usual level is the median, the middle value, which one wild year cannot drag. The further a month sits from it, the higher its level:
after: Safeguard: where fires are rare (fewer than 5 a month), a country stays 'normal'. Three fires instead of one is not an alert.

sections.title: Conditions and land cover
body: Temperature and rain are NASA POWER monthly values at the four busiest fire areas of each country, compared with the same month over 2001–2024.
'What burned' places every detection on the MODIS land cover map of its year: forest, shrub and savanna, cropland or other.
These are conditions seen at the time, not proof of a cause: most fires are lit by people.

sections.title: Limits
body: A detection is not a burned area: a large fire can make hundreds of detections, a small one none.
Clouds and thick smoke hide fires, and the satellites pass only a few times a day, so short fires can be missed.
Small farm fires often fall below what MODIS can see. VIIRS catches more of them.
The FIRMS history here covers 2020–2024, so each month is compared with only 4 other years. The usual level is still fragile.
The satellite orbits on the globe are drawn to explain how MODIS scans; they are not live positions.

steps.name: Detect
steps.line: NASA satellites flag every hot point on the ground. FIRMS publishes them, MODIS and VIIRS.

steps.name: Clean
steps.line: We keep vegetation fires only: no factories, no gas flares, no low-confidence points.

steps.name: Remember
steps.line: Each month is set against the same month in the other years. The fire season is built in.

steps.name: Rank
steps.line: The further a month sits from its usual level, the higher it ranks.

steps.name: Tell
steps.line: One word, one colour, one sentence. That is the bulletin.

doAlert: Do not burn waste, stubble or brush, and do not light fires outdoors.
Report smoke or flames at once to the emergency number.
Know two ways out of your area. Keep a bag ready: water, medicines, documents, phone charger.
Clear dry leaves and brush from around buildings.
If the authorities tell you to leave, leave early.
doCalm: Clear dry vegetation around buildings before the season starts.
Find out how your local authority sends fire alerts, and sign up.
Agree with your household where to meet and which road to take.
safety.guideNote: General wildfire guidance, not NASA data. Your civil protection authority comes first.
